follow100Note: Costs ran to $105.90 per $100 of revenue — the extra is the loss, covered by cash the company already had.

kpis.note: vs a year ago; includes $388M from CyberArk and Chronosphere

kpis.label: Adj. free cash flow
kpis.note: in the quarter; operating cash flow was $871M

oneTimers: Share-based compensation was $517M, acquisition-related costs $198M and amortization of acquired intangible assets $280M — together they are the entire gap between the $177M GAAP net loss and $684M of non-GAAP net income.
Acquisitions did heavy lifting: CyberArk and Chronosphere contributed $388M of the quarter's revenue, $1.6B of Next-Generation Security ARR and $1.8B of remaining performance obligations.
Excluding one-offs and stock pay, Palo Alto earned $684M (non-GAAP) — the underlying business was profitable even as GAAP showed a loss.
otherDetail: Other income, net of $27M, with no interest expense in the quarter.

segments.name: Subscription & support
segments.note: Security subscriptions and support — the recurring core of the business, now including CyberArk identity security.

takeaways.text: Revenue grew 31% to $3.0B — but $388M of it came from the newly acquired CyberArk and Chronosphere, so organic growth was slower than the headline.
takeaways.title: Growth, much of it bought

takeaways.text: Next-Generation Security ARR grew 60% to $8.1B (including $1.6B from the acquisitions), and remaining performance obligations rose 36% to $18.4B.
takeaways.title: The platform bet is working

takeaways.text: GAAP showed a $177M loss, driven by $517M of stock pay and $478M of acquisition costs and amortization. Operating cash flow was $871M in the same quarter — the loss consumed no cash.
takeaways.title: A paper loss, not a cash loss

verdict: Palo Alto Networks grew revenue 31% to $3.0B with help from CyberArk, but $995M of stock pay and deal costs flipped the quarter to a $177M GAAP loss.
